beats.narration: Sprout's main loop checks the button over and over, millions of times a second. Ninety-nine point nine nine percent of those checks find nothing.
It is like checking your front door every second in case a parcel arrived.
Is that bad? It works.
It works, but it wastes energy, and when the loop gets busy, a quick press can be missed entirely.
There is a better way: let the hardware tap the processor on the shoulder.
That tap is called an interrupt. Today's episode is about how interrupts work, why they are wonderful, and why they cause some of the strangest bugs in all of programming.
An interrupt is a signal from hardware that says, stop what you are doing, something needs attention now.
The processor pauses its current work, runs a special function, then resumes exactly where it left off.
That special function is the interrupt service routine, or ISR. The main code does not call it. The hardware does, whenever the event happens.
So the doorbell rings, you answer the door, sign for the parcel, and go back to your book, at exactly the same page.
Almost every peripheral can raise an interrupt. Each source is identified by a number, often called the interrupt request number, or IRQ.

beats.narration: What if two interrupts arrive at once? Or a new one arrives while a handler is running? The interrupt controller decides, using priorities.
Higher priority interrupts are served first. And on many chips, a higher priority interrupt can interrupt a lower priority handler that is already running. That is called nesting.
The main code is interrupted by the button handler, which is itself interrupted by the tank empty handler. When that finishes, the button handler resumes, and then main.
Like a meeting about a meeting, interrupted by an emergency.
Nesting keeps urgent work fast, but each nested level uses more stack memory, and it makes timing harder to reason about. Use priorities thoughtfully, not generously.
For the main code to resume as if nothing happened, the processor must save its exact state before running the handler.
That means the registers it was using, and the address of the next instruction.
On many modern microcontrollers, the hardware saves the most important registers automatically, which is why you can write handlers as ordinary C functions.
The lookup step uses the vector table: a list of addresses stored at a known place in memory, one entry per interrupt.
Entry number seven might point to the timer handler, entry twelve to the serial handler.
And if an interrupt fires that has no handler?
Then the table points to a default handler, which usually just loops forever.
A chip that mysteriously freezes is often stuck in a default handler for an interrupt someone enabled by accident.
Here is our button handler. Its name matches an entry in the vector table. First, it clears the interrupt's pending flag.

beats.narration: Now for the dangerous part. The handler and the main code share data. And sharing data between them, carelessly, is how ghosts get into machines.
Ghosts?
Bugs that appear once a week, cannot be reproduced, and vanish when you add a print statement. Watch this.
In the main loop, this one line is really three steps: read presses, subtract, write the result back.

beats.narration: The fix is a critical section: a short stretch of code during which interrupts are temporarily disabled, so the read-modify-write cannot be split.
Disable, update, restore. Keep it as short as possible, because while interrupts are off, the whole system is deaf.
And restore the previous state, rather than blindly enabling. If interrupts were already off when you started, you should leave them off.
Some updates are atomic, meaning the processor completes them in one indivisible step, like writing a single aligned thirty-two bit value on a thirty-two bit chip.
But read-modify-write sequences, and anything larger than the processor's native size, usually are not.
Getting an interrupt to fire takes several layers of permission. Miss one, and nothing happens, with no error to tell you why.
The peripheral must be told to generate the event, like a falling edge on pin three. The interrupt controller must enable that IRQ number, with a priority.
And interrupts must be enabled globally.
And the handler must be named exactly right, or the vector table will not point to it. One typo, and the default handler eats your interrupt.
The order matters too. Clear any stale pending flag before enabling, or an old event from power-up will fire immediately and confuse everyone.
There is one more choice when configuring a pin interrupt: edge or level. An edge-triggered interrupt fires once, at the moment the signal changes.
A level-triggered one keeps firing for as long as the signal stays in its active state.
Buttons and most pins use edges.
Level triggering suits devices that hold a line active until they are serviced, like a sensor that keeps its alert line low until you read its data.
Get it backwards, and a level interrupt that is never cleared at the source will fire endlessly, and the main loop never runs again.
The board looks dead, but it is really just extremely busy.
Interrupts are amazing. Let us use them for everything.
Please do not. Interrupts have costs. Every one adds a little overhead, and a system with too many becomes hard to predict.
If something happens very frequently, like a sensor that changes every few microseconds, an interrupt per change could overwhelm the processor. Polling it at a steady rate is calmer.
A noisy, bouncing button is another case. Each bounce fires an interrupt. Many designs poll buttons from a regular timer instead, which debounces naturally.
And sometimes the simplest loop is the right answer. If Sprout checks the soil once a minute, nobody needs an interrupt for that.
Cy wants a number. How long between the button press and the handler running? That delay is called interrupt latency.
The hardware part is usually tiny, a few dozen clock cycles. At eight megahertz, that is a handful of microseconds.
The big, unpredictable part is software: other handlers running, and critical sections where interrupts are switched off.
That is why critical sections must be short. The longest stretch of code with interrupts disabled sets a floor on the worst case latency of every interrupt in the system.
And we can measure it. Wire the button to one scope channel. In the handler, set a spare pin high on the first line.
The gap between the two edges is the real latency.
Six microseconds, typically. Thirty in the worst case, when the serial handler was busy. For a button, that is instant. For a motor, it might matter.

One interrupt is used by almost every embedded system: the system tick. A timer fires at a steady rate, often a thousand times a second, and the handler simply counts.
Now any code can ask what time it is, in milliseconds since boot. And it can check whether enough time has passed without blocking.

beats.narration: With a tick, we can build a tiny scheduler: a table of tasks, each with a period. The main loop runs each task when its time comes.
The button is polled every ten milliseconds, the LED updated four times a second, the soil checked every minute. Each task runs briefly and returns.

To recap. An interrupt lets hardware pause your program, run a handler, and resume. Priorities decide who goes first, and higher priorities can nest inside lower ones.
